s: Marine park off Saadiyat Island · reefs, seagrass, dolphins and hawksbill turtles
el: 59 km², incl. 7 km² of coral reef
se: Just off Abu Dhabi city, coral reefs and seagrass meadows shelter dolphins, green turtles and critically endangered hawksbill turtles
sa: على مقربة من مدينة أبوظبي تؤوي الشعاب المرجانية ومروج الأعشاب البحرية الدلافين والسلاحف الخضراء وسلاحف منقار الصقر المهددة بالانقراض بشدة
desc: A marine national park off Saadiyat Island in Abu Dhabi, declared in 2017 and covering 59 km². It includes about 7 km² of coral reefs and 8 km² of seagrass. Recorded fauna include 24 bird, 13 reptile and 5 mammal species, 28 of them threatened, among them dolphins, green turtles, sea snakes and the critically endangered hawksbill turtle. It is one of six marine areas in the Sheikh Zayed Protected Areas Network managed by the Environment Agency – Abu Dhabi.
sig: A coral and seagrass refuge for threatened turtles right beside a capital city.
ex: EAD; Gulf News (2022); Abu Dhabi Maritime MPA Guide 2020

s: Sixteen desert and marine reserves of the Sheikh Zayed Protected Areas Network · oryx, houbara, dugongs
dr: Al Yasat MPA 2005; four new reserves 2025; others not dated in the EAD list
te: From oryx dunes to coral islands
ta: من كثبان المها إلى الجزر المرجانية
se: Abu Dhabi protects dunes where Arabian oryx roam, nesting grounds of the houbara and coral islands visited by dugongs
sa: تحمي أبوظبي كثبانًا يجول فيها المها العربي، ومواطن تعشيش الحبارى، وجزرًا مرجانية يرتادها الأطوم
desc: This record groups 16 reserves of the Sheikh Zayed Protected Areas Network: Al Yasat Marine Protected Area (2005, 2,256 km²), Al Bidaa, Al Dilfawiya (186 km² per WDPA), Al Ramlah (544 km²), Qasr Al Sarab (expanded 2025), the Arabian Oryx Protected Area (5,975 km², the world's largest Arabian oryx population), Al Ghada (Al Marzoum), Bu Al Dibsa (Yaw Al Dibsa), Al Houbara, Bida Hazza, Barqa Al Suqoor, Al Tawi (more than 46 km²), and four reserves designated in October 2025: Liwa Groundwater Reservoir Reserve, Ghaf Natural Reserve, Abu Al Abyad Marine Reserve and Sir Bani Yas and Desert Islands Marine Reserve. The EAD list does not give declaration years for most members. The October 2025 expansion added 4,581 km² and brought the network to 26 protected areas covering 22,821 km², with a target of 20% of the emirate's land.
sig: Abu Dhabi's reserve network protects the emirate's main desert, groundwater and marine habitats, including key oryx, houbara and dugong areas.

s: Four Dubai desert and mountain reserves · Al Marmoom, Al Wohoosh, Jabal Nazwa, Ghaf Nazwa
dr: Declared by decree 2014; Al Marmoom launched January 2018
el: Al Marmoom covers about 10% of Dubai
se: Dubai's inland reserves protect desert lakes full of flamingos, ghaf woodland and the rocky hill of Jabal Nazwa
sa: تحمي محميات دبي الداخلية بحيرات صحراوية تعجّ بطيور الفلامنغو، وغابات الغاف، وتلال جبل نزوى الصخرية
desc: This record groups four of Dubai's eight protected areas: Al Marmoom Desert Conservation Reserve, Al Wohoosh Desert Conservation Reserve, Jabal Nazwa Conservation Reserve and Ghaf Nazwa Conservation Reserve. Their boundaries were set by a decree of the Ruler of Dubai announced in May 2014, and Dubai Municipality manages them; the eight reserves cover about 31% of the emirate. Al Marmoom was launched in January 2018 as the UAE's first unfenced conservation reserve, covering about 10% of Dubai, with the Al Qudra lakes, 26 reptile, 9 mammal and 39 plant species and flocks of 300 to 500 flamingos. The reserves were set up to protect desert plants such as samar, ghaf and sidr.
sig: Dubai's inland reserves keep large tracts of desert, ghaf woodland and desert lakes protected next to a fast-growing city.

s: Nine Sharjah desert, mountain, mangrove and marine reserves · from ghaf belts to Khor Fakkan reefs
el: Al Muntather planted with over a million ghaf and sidr trees
te: A million trees in the desert
se: Sharjah protects a green belt of a million ghaf and sidr trees, desert reserves, mangroves at Al Hamriyah and a marine reserve at Khor Fakkan
sa: تحمي الشارقة حزامًا أخضر من مليون شجرة غاف وسدر، ومحميات صحراوية، وأشجار القرم في الحمرية، ومحمية بحرية في خورفكان
desc: This record groups nine Sharjah reserves managed by the Environment and Protected Areas Authority: Al Bridi (listed as 18.5 km² in 2007; Decree No. 44 of 2018), Al Dhulaima (2007, 0.96 km²), Al Faya (2007), Al Muntather (Decree No. 54 of 2022; merged with Mahafiz in December 2025), Al Mutasannad (renamed from Musannad in December 2025), Shanuf, Wadi Al Qarha (April 2026), Al Hamriyah Mangroves (Decree No. 53 of 2022) and Al Qalqali Marine Reserve at Khor Fakkan (November 2025). Al Muntather is a desert green belt in the Al Bataeh area planted with more than a million ghaf and sidr trees. The decrees ban hunting, introducing alien species, cutting trees and building without a permit, and protect all species using the reserves.
sig: Sharjah has built a growing network of small reserves covering desert, woodland, mountain, mangrove and marine habitats.
disc: Al Muntather: over a million ghaf and sidr trees

s: Ramsar mudflats west of Musaffah · flamingo breeding record and threatened turtles
ta: حيث عشّش ألفا زوج من الفلامنغو
se: Tidal mudflats near Abu Dhabi where flamingos once raised 801 chicks and more than 80 kinds of birds feed
sa: سهول طينية مدّية قرب أبوظبي فقس فيها ذات مرة 801 فرخ فلامنغو، وتقتات فيها أكثر من 80 نوعًا من الطيور
desc: A coastal wetland of 14,504.5 ha west of the Musaffah channel, about 20 km from Abu Dhabi city, designated as Ramsar site no. 2293 on 27 September 2016. Habitats include mangroves, salt marshes, seagrass beds and tidal mudflats that support more than 80 migratory and resident bird species. In 2009 it hosted a record greater flamingo breeding event of 2,000 pairs and 801 hatchlings. Threatened species include hawksbill and green turtles, greater spotted eagle, Socotra cormorant and dugong.
sig: One of the Arabian Gulf's key flamingo breeding wetlands, beside a major industrial city.
refs: Ramsar Sites Information Service. Bul Syayeef (site no. 2293). https://rsis.ramsar.org/ris/2293

s: Ramsar mountain wetland in the Hajar ophiolite · rare freshwater habitat
dr: Dubai reserve 2014; Ramsar site no. 2368, 9 January 2019
se: In the Hajar Mountains of Hatta, rare freshwater pools shelter dragonflies, fish and amphibians, while Arabian tahr live on the slopes
sa: في جبال الحجر بحتا تؤوي برك المياه العذبة النادرة اليعاسيب والأسماك والبرمائيات، فيما يعيش الطهر العربي على السفوح
desc: A 2,100 ha reserve in the Hajar Mountains of Dubai, part of the Oman–UAE ophiolite, designated as Ramsar site no. 2368 on 9 January 2019. It is a rare mountain freshwater ecosystem; the mountains receive about 30% of the country's annual rainfall, recharging the aquifer that feeds the Hatta and Al Ghabra dams. The site supports 19% of the country's plant species, 79% of its dragonfly species, 27% of its bird species and 44% of its mammal species. Threatened species include the Arabian leopard, Arabian tahr and Egyptian vulture.
sig: A rare freshwater mountain wetland that concentrates much of the UAE's biodiversity in a small area.
refs: Ramsar Sites Information Service. Hatta Mountain Reserve (site no. 2368). https://rsis.ramsar.org/ris/2368

s: Ramsar marine sanctuary · Dubai's only hawksbill turtle nesting beaches
se: Between Palm Jebel Ali and Abu Dhabi, the only beaches in Dubai where hawksbill turtles still lay their eggs
sa: بين نخلة جبل علي وحدود أبوظبي تمتد الشواطئ الوحيدة في دبي التي ما زالت سلاحف منقار الصقر تضع فيها بيضها
desc: A 2,002 ha coastal and marine sanctuary from Palm Jebel Ali south-west to the Abu Dhabi border, designated as Ramsar site no. 2364 on 25 October 2018 and part of the Jabal Ali Marine Sanctuary, an Ecologically or Biologically Significant Marine Area under the CBD. Habitats include coral reefs, mangroves, shallow lagoons, seagrass and oyster beds and sandy shores, sheltering over 500 marine species. Its beaches are the only hawksbill turtle breeding grounds in the emirate, with 30 nests recorded in 2017. Seagrass beds feed green turtles and dugongs.
sig: The last natural stretch of Dubai's coast, critical for nesting hawksbill turtles.

s: Ramsar inland wetland in Sharjah · a former tidal lagoon with 144 bird species
dr: Sharjah reserve 2007; Ramsar site no. 2386, 9 May 2019
te: A lagoon left behind by the sea
se: Once a tidal lagoon, Wasit is now an inland wetland in Sharjah where at least 144 kinds of birds have been seen
sa: كانت واسط بحيرة مدّية، وهي اليوم أرض رطبة داخلية في الشارقة رُصد فيها ما لا يقل عن 144 نوعًا من الطيور
desc: An 86 ha inland lake and wetland complex about 15 km from the coast and Sharjah city, designated as Ramsar site no. 2386 on 9 May 2019. It was once a tidal lagoon, which makes it useful for understanding how the coastline has changed. Mudflats, lakes, dunes, reed beds and thickets support at least 144 bird species, many of them migrants, including near-threatened curlew sandpiper, bar-tailed and black-tailed godwits and Eurasian curlew, and the vulnerable Socotra cormorant. It was designated a protected area by the Ruler of Sharjah in 2007.
sig: A rare urban-edge wetland that records the former shoreline of Sharjah.
refs: Ramsar Sites Information Service. Wasit Nature Reserve (site no. 2386). https://rsis.ramsar.org/ris/2386

s: Mountain tombs, villages and falaj of Hatta · Bronze Age to Islamic periods
el: Over 70 tombs at Jabal al Yamh
se: Above Hatta, more than seventy stone tombs line the ridge, and below them lie old stone villages and a water channel 560 m long
sa: فوق حتا تصطف على الجبل أكثر من سبعين مدفنًا حجريًا، وتحتها قرى حجرية قديمة وقناة فلج يبلغ طولها نحو 560 مترًا
desc: A UNESCO Tentative List property (2023) in the Hatta enclave of Dubai, where 22 archaeological sites have been identified, documented and mapped. The Jabal al Yamh necropolis has over 70 tombs spread over about 4 km, mostly in the Hafit style with others of Umm an-Nar, Wadi Suq and Iron Age type, some reused into the Middle Islamic period. Suhaila 1 was occupied from the early Islamic era to the mid-20th century, while Suhaila 2 and Wadi Jeema are larger settlements with agricultural terraces. An underground falaj about 560 m long dates to the 1st millennium BCE.
sig: A mountain landscape showing continuous use of the Hajar valleys from the Early Bronze Age to the recent past.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2023). Hatta Archaeological Landscape (Emirate of Dubai), Tentative List ref. 6664. https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/6664
conf: t0 is an estimate for the start of the Early Bronze Age (Hafit period, c. 3200 BC); t1 reflects abandonment in the mid-20th century

s: Traditional merchants' harbour · dhows, abras, souqs and wind-tower quarters
el: Creek about 14 km long; property covers the first 4.5 km
se: Wooden abras still ferry people across the creek where about 800 people settled in 1833 and dhows have traded ever since
sa: ما زالت العبرات الخشبية تنقل الناس عبر الخور الذي استقر عند مصبه نحو 800 شخص عام 1833، ولا تزال المراكب الشراعية تتاجر فيه
desc: Khor Dubai is a natural seawater inlet of the Arabian Gulf about 14 km long and 100 to 500 m wide, dividing Bur Dubai and Deira and ending at Ras Al Khor. Dubai is first recorded by the Venetian pearl merchant Gasparo Balbi in 1587, and in 1833 about 800 members of the Bani Yas settled at the creek mouth. The creek was dredged in 1961 to admit vessels drawing 2.1 m. The Tentative List property covers the first 4.5 km, including Shindagha, Bastakia with its wind-towers, the Deira souqs and Al Fahidi Fort.
sig: A living traditional harbour where dhow trade and abra crossings continue at the core of a global city.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2012). Khor Dubai (Dubai Creek), a traditional merchants' harbour, Tentative List ref. 5662. https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5662

s: Four-domed stone-and-mud mosque · oldest mosque in the UAE still in use
el: 6.8 × 6.8 m, four domes on one pillar
se: A small square mosque in Fujairah whose four domes rest on a single stone pillar, still used for prayer after about 500 years
sa: مسجد مربع صغير في الفجيرة تستند قبابه الأربع إلى عمود حجري واحد، وما زالت الصلاة تقام فيه منذ نحو خمسة قرون
desc: A small square mosque of stone and mud in Al Bidya, Fujairah, measuring 6.8 × 6.8 m, with four domes of unequal size supported by one central pillar. Radiocarbon dating of charcoal from the foundation gives a construction window of 1450–1670 AD (95% probability) and 1480–1650 AD (68%). The walls have dentate carvings, light openings and lamp niches; the mihrab is 180 cm high and 90 cm wide. It is described as the oldest mosque in the UAE still in use, and watchtowers, house foundations and petroglyphs lie nearby.
sig: A rare surviving pre-modern mosque of the east coast that is still in daily use.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2012). Al Bidya Mosque, Tentative List ref. 5665. https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/5665
conf: t0 uses the earliest end of the 95% radiocarbon range (1450 AD)

n: Pearl trading town of Jazirat Al Hamra
s: Abandoned coral-stone pearling town · houses, souq, mosques and fort
el: 45 ha former island; about 500 houses in 1908
te: The town the pearl divers left
se: A whole town of coral-stone houses in Ras Al Khaimah, built on pearling and left almost untouched since its people moved out around 1970
sa: بلدة كاملة من بيوت الحجر المرجاني في رأس الخيمة، قامت على الغوص على اللؤلؤ وبقيت على حالها تقريبًا منذ رحيل أهلها نحو عام 1970
desc: A former 45 ha island in a lagoon on the southern coast of Ras Al Khaimah, thought to date from the 17th century as it is absent from Gasparo Balbi's 1580 list. It was first described in 1756, mapped by the British in 1820, and in 1908 J.G. Lorimer counted 500 houses in two quarters, the main town of the Za'ab tribe who lived mainly from pearl diving. Houses of coral stone and fossil beach rock, a souq, mosques and a fort survive, including the two-storey Bait Omran and the wind-tower house of Bait Abdul Karim. Its inhabitants left between 1968 and 1971.
sig: One of the best-preserved traditional pearling towns of the Arabian Gulf coast.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2020). The pearl trading town of Jazirat Al-Hamra, Tentative List ref. 6464. https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/6464

s: Fort mound on Dibba Bay · Neolithic to 20th century, Qasimi governor's seat
te: A fort built on thousands of years
se: Under the fort of Dibba Al-Hisn lie layers from the Stone Age to the last century, with glass workshops, date presses and a fish factory
sa: تحت حصن دبا الحصن طبقات تمتد من العصر الحجري الحديث إلى القرن الماضي، فيها ورش للزجاج ومدابس للتمر ومصنع للسمك المملح
desc: The northern component of the Coastal Fortified Network of South Eastern Arabia, on Dibba Bay at the southern edge of the Musandam Peninsula. The fort mound has a stratigraphic sequence from the Neolithic to the 20th century, with three circular bastion foundations, glass-working workshops, twelve madabis for date processing, pearl-processing installations and a 19th-century salted fish factory. Portuguese forces reportedly seized the site in 1624 CE, a phase known from maps but not yet confirmed by excavation. The surviving fabric is mainly Qasimi, and the fort served as a governor's residence and court in the 19th and 20th centuries.
sig: Part of a chain of east-coast forts tracing the shift from Hormuzi trade to Portuguese and then Al Qasimi control.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2026). Coastal Fortified Network of South Eastern Arabia, Tentative List ref. 7039 (submitted 28/07/2026). https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/7039/
conf: t0 is a broad estimate for the Neolithic start of the sequence (not dated in the source); the header coordinate is used (the component text gives a garbled seconds value)

s: East and West forts and walled old town · Portuguese, Arab and Qasimi phases
se: On Khor Fakkan's bay, one fort was rebuilt three times, by the Portuguese, by Arab rulers and by the Qawasim
sa: على خليج خورفكان أُعيد بناء حصن واحد ثلاث مرات: على يد البرتغاليين، ثم الحكام العرب، ثم القواسم
desc: The central component of the Coastal Fortified Network of South Eastern Arabia, on a sheltered crescent bay of the Sea of Oman. The East Fort is a stone enclosure with three towers and an Arabic inscription recording the Qasimi takeover. The West Fort has three superimposed phases: a triangular plan interpreted as 17th-century Portuguese, a rectangular structure of the later 18th century and a square fort with a round tower of the 19th century. The old town has occupation layers and stone houses of the 15th to early 16th centuries and a surviving medieval town wall more than 155 m long; a Portuguese fort was built here in 1620 CE.
sig: A layered harbour fortification recording three centuries of contest over the Sea of Oman coast.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2026). Coastal Fortified Network of South Eastern Arabia, Tentative List ref. 7039 (submitted 28/07/2026). https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/7039/
conf: t0 approximates the 15th-century old town (c. 1450); t1 approximates the 19th-century Qasimi fort

s: Portuguese rammed-earth fort at the Khor Kalba creek · later Qasimi fort
el: Quadrangular fort with two round corner towers
te: The Portuguese fort by the mangroves
se: At the mouth of the mangrove creek of Kalba, the Portuguese built a rammed-earth fort in 1624, later abandoned, perhaps as the creek silted up
sa: عند مصب خور كلباء بين أشجار القرم بنى البرتغاليون عام 1624 حصنًا من التراب المدكوك، هُجر لاحقًا، ربما حين امتلأ الخور بالطمي
desc: The southern component of the Coastal Fortified Network of South Eastern Arabia, on a sandy plain at the mouth of the Khor Kalba tidal creek and mangrove lagoon. Under the Kingdom of Hormuz it was a fortified settlement governed by a Qasimi chief before Portuguese forces seized it in 1624 CE. The Portuguese built a rammed-earth fort on stone foundations, used as a navigation aid, trading station and supply depot; excavations show a quadrangular enclosure with two circular corner towers and a south entrance. It was probably abandoned in the 18th century, possibly as the creek silted, and a later fort to the north-east reflects Al Qasimi consolidation in the 18th and 19th centuries.
sig: Archaeological evidence of the Portuguese supply network on the Sea of Oman coast and its Qasimi successor.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2026). Coastal Fortified Network of South Eastern Arabia, Tentative List ref. 7039 (submitted 28/07/2026). https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/7039/
conf: t0 uses the 1624 seizure (the earlier Hormuzi settlement is undated); t1 approximates the 19th-century Qasimi fort; the header coordinate is used (the component text gives a garbled seconds value)

s: First rock art site found in the Hajar Mountains · extinct wild asses and ibex
p: 5th millennium BCE – 2nd millennium BCE and later
se: Near Kalba, people carved wild asses that no longer exist, then ibex over them, thousands of years ago
sa: قرب كلباء نقش الناس قبل آلاف السنين صور حمير برية لم تعد موجودة، ثم نقشوا فوقها صور الوعول
desc: A rock art site near Kalba and the border with Oman, the first rock art site discovered in the Hajar Mountains and a component of The Rock Art of the Emirate of Sharjah on the UNESCO Tentative List (2023). The oldest phase, around the 5th millennium BCE, shows wild asses, probably the extinct Syrian wild ass (Equus hemionus hemippus). These are overlain by 4th-millennium BCE ibex or wild goats in the three-strokes style, and a third phase of the 3rd–2nd millennium BCE and later adds abstract designs and human figures. It also has naturalistic, dynamic animal figures not found elsewhere in the region.
sig: A long, layered record of prehistoric art and of a wild ass now extinct.
disc: First Hajar rock art site found
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2023). The Rock Art of the Emirate of Sharjah, Tentative List ref. 6642. https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/6642

s: Offshore salt-dome island · top UAE hawksbill nesting site and seabird colonies
dr: Protected 2000; Ramsar site no. 2191 (2013); UNESCO Tentative List 2012
se: Far out in the Arabian Gulf, this colourful salt-dome island is where more hawksbill turtles nest than anywhere else in the UAE
sa: في عرض الخليج العربي تقع هذه الجزيرة الملحية الملوّنة التي تعشّش فيها سلاحف منقار الصقر أكثر من أي مكان آخر في الإمارات
desc: An offshore island about 110 km from Sharjah formed by a mineral-rich salt dome, whose iron oxide and sulfur were mined in the past. Protected by Decree No. 25 of 2000, it was listed as Ramsar site no. 2191 on 2 December 2013 (4,964 ha, including 1,333 ha of land) and placed on the UNESCO Tentative List in 2012. It is the UAE's most important hawksbill turtle nesting site and supports nesting Socotra cormorants, red-billed tropicbirds, terns and more than 1% of the regional sooty gull breeding population. Ramsar records 40 coral and 76 reef fish species, and pottery about 3,500 years old has been found there.
sig: A rare combination of salt-dome geology, turtle nesting beaches, seabird colonies and coral reefs.
ex: UNESCO Tentative List 5661; Ramsar annotated summary (2191)

s: Bronze Age copper mining and smelting valley in the Hajar ophiolite
se: In Wadi Al Helo, Bronze Age people dug copper from hard rock and smelted it in furnaces set high up to catch the wind
sa: في وادي الحلو استخرج أهل العصر البرونزي النحاس من صخر صلب، وصهروه في أفران أقاموها في الأعالي لتلتقط الريح
desc: A valley of about 84 km² in the Hajar Mountains of Sharjah, listed on the UNESCO Tentative List in 2023 as testimony of Bronze Age copper production in south-east Arabia. Copper was mined in open workings in hard ophiolite and smelted in furnaces placed on high ground to use the wind, fuelled by acacia wood. Remains include slag heaps, workshops, a casting pit and a watchtower at the valley entrance. The dossier links it to Bronze Age centres such as Tell Abraq, Kalba and Umm an-Nar, and rock art in the valley includes T-shaped figures, boats and Syrian wild asses.
sig: A key source landscape for the copper trade of ancient Magan.
disc: Linked to Tell Abraq and Umm an-Nar
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (2023). Wadi Al Helo: Testimony of Bronze Age Copper Production, Tentative List ref. 6641. https://whc.unesco.org/fr/listesindicatives/6641
The National (28 February 2023). Four sites in Sharjah added to Unesco tentative list. https://www.thenationalnews.com/uae/2023/02/28/four-sites-in-sharjah-added-to-unesco-tentative-list
conf: The source gives no dates; t0/t1 are a broad estimate for the Bronze Age in south-east Arabia (c. 3200–1300 BC). Wadi Al Helo is also a Sharjah nature reserve

s: Falaj-fed palm oasis of Al Ain · forts, mosques and watchtower
dr: UNESCO World Heritage 2011 (component of Cultural Sites of Al Ain)
se: In Al Jimi Oasis a 14 m tower guarded the spot where the falaj water came up for people to drink
sa: في واحة الجيمي كان برج بارتفاع 14 مترًا يحرس الموضع الذي تظهر فيه مياه الفلج ليشرب منها الناس
desc: One of the six oases of the Cultural Sites of Al Ain World Heritage property, covering about 80 ha in a sunken basin divided into 185 palm-garden plots irrigated by a falaj. More than a dozen historic earthen buildings, including mosques, fortified houses and watchtowers, show its importance from the 18th century onward. The largest is the fortified house of Ahmad bin Hilal Al Dhaheri, governor of Al Ain from 1896 to 1937. The 14 m Jimi watchtower guarded the shariaa, where the falaj water reached the surface.
sig: A living oasis that shows how falaj irrigation and fortified houses sustained life in Al Ain.
refs: UNESCO World Heritage Centre. Cultural Sites of Al Ain (Hafit, Hili, Bidaa Bint Saud and Oases Areas), ref. 1343 (inscribed 2011). https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1343/

s: Rocky ridge with Al Naqfa Fort ruins · commands the approach to Al Ain Oasis
dr: UNESCO World Heritage 2011 (component of Cultural Sites of Al Ain)
se: From this rocky ridge a fort watched over the road into Al Ain Oasis for more than three thousand years
sa: من هذا المرتفع الصخري راقب حصنٌ الطريق المؤدي إلى واحة العين، وتشهد كسر الفخار على ارتياده منذ أكثر من ثلاثة آلاف عام
desc: A component of the Cultural Sites of Al Ain World Heritage property, where the ruins of Al Naqfa Fort stand on a rocky outcrop overlooking and commanding the approach to Al Ain Oasis. Surface pottery dates from the Iron Age (1300–300 BCE) through the Late Islamic period (1650–1950 CE). A modern cemetery and communal prayer ground nearby show its continuing importance.
sig: A strategic lookout showing long use of the ridges that guard the Al Ain oases.
disc: Iron Age to Late Islamic pottery

s: Early Bronze Age beehive tombs north of Jebel Hafit · Hafit period
dr: UNESCO World Heritage 2011 (component of Cultural Sites of Al Ain)
el: Tombs up to about 8 m high
se: On the ridges north of Jebel Hafit, round stone tombs about 5,000 years old held a few people each
sa: على التلال شمال جبل حفيت مدافن حجرية مستديرة عمرها نحو خمسة آلاف عام، ضمّ كل منها بضعة أشخاص
desc: One of four Hafit tomb sites in the Jebel Hafit area included in the Cultural Sites of Al Ain World Heritage property, assigned to the Hafit period (c. 3200–2700 BCE). Hafit tombs are round single-chamber towers up to about 8 m high and 5–7 m across, with two or three concentric ring walls and an entrance, usually holding 3–4 individuals. Grave goods include imported ceramic vessels, copper objects, beads and occasional shell and flint artefacts; about 50 Mesopotamian vessels have been recovered from Hafit tombs, mostly at Jebel Hafit and Garn Bint Saud.
sig: Early Bronze Age monuments that mark the first contacts of the Al Ain area with Mesopotamia.
disc: About 50 Mesopotamian vessels from Hafit tombs
